Midstream Air

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Residents of the upmarket Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand thought they were buying into a dream lifestyle ... until gases and the stench from a private landfill site started affecting their quality of life and their health.
Residents of these estates and surrounding areas in Olifantsfontein and Tembisa in Midrand, have been battling for more than two years to get Interwaste to address the dangerous gases emanating from its FG Landfill site in Midrand. The source of the problem is said to be mining waste from Lonmin and possibly other mines being dumped at the landfill site. The gases being emitted from the site include hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide.
Those living in the area say the stench is so bad on some days that they have to fight the urge to throw up. They say they suffer regular respiratory illnesses and ailments such as nose bleeds.
Lanette Hughes, who is spearheading residents' battle, says her two young children are often sick, her childhood asthma has returned and they have needed to buy air purifiers for their home.
Another resident says her family suffers so much that they are nearly exclusively living in one room in their house that has an air purifier installed.
Hughes and her team of volunteers are using technology to their advantage and have created an online tracker for people to record complaints. Between May 2016 and February 2017, there were a total of 4582 complaints logged. A record number of 919 complaints were logged from Midstream Estate between 1 and 13 February.
They have also taken their woes to the Public Protector, where an agreement was reached in October 2016 and Interwaste, the Department of Environmental Affairs and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development were asked to make commitments to address the problems. But residents say that the commitments are not begin honoured and the situation is now worse than ever.
In an attempt to work with Interwaste to solve the problems, the developers of the Midstream Estate, Bondev, purchased machinery to measure the gases in the air.
Residents say that the steps that have been taken to address the problems are not working because Interwaste is not taking the necessary steps. They say, for instance, that the flares installed to burn off the gases do not have the required scrubbers installed.

Summary:
Who ensures the quality of the air we breathe? This is a question that residents of the Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand, Olifantsfontein and Tembisa are asking themselves in their battle for clean air.
They say the Department of environmental Affairs (DEA) and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (GDARD) is letting them down by not clamping down on Interwaste's FG Landfill site in Midrand. They say the landfill site is emitting dangerous gases and bad odours into the air and not taking the necessary steps to prevent harm to the health of people living in the area.
The large private landfill site accepts waste from mining operations by Lonmin and possibly other mine groups.
Let alone the bad smell, residents say they suffer respiratory illnesses, nose bleeds and more. They have to take their children to the doctor numerous time a month. Many have costly air purifiers in their homes.
An online tracking tool developed by those spearheading the battle has recorded more than 4000 complaints in less than a year.
Section 24 of the Bill of Rights in the South African Constitution guarantees everyone the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being.
Residents first started complaining to the DEA and GDARD in 2014 but, dissatisfied with what they saw as a lack of action, a group of residents took their case to the Public Protector's Office, which facilitated an agreement between the parties in November 2016. But, say residents, the pollution is now worse than ever and the monthly feedback meetings promised by the DEA have not happened. The DEA and GDARD were also supposed to provide the Public Protector's Office with regular feedback.
We aim to interview residents of the area, representatives of the DEA and GDARD, Interwaste (owners of the landfill) and an independent air quality scientist.

Press Release:


Battle To Breathe
An epic battle is set to play out in courtrooms as frustrated Midrand residents take on a waste dump in the area. Claiming a range of health problems as a result of air pollution, possibly from landfill gases, communities used app technology and social media to record their complaints and compel authorities to take action. The landfill's owners are not taking it lying down. Carte Blanche examines the issues.



PROMOS:

10 secs
Midrand residents celebrated when the Green Scorpions ordered the local landfill to stop receiving waste – but it’s gloves off as the owners challenge the move.

15 secs
GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: You have landfills all across the country...but you don’t have the impacts that we’re seeing now.
In Midrand, residents and the local landfill do battle over claims that gasses from dump are making people sick...who will win the fight?

15 secs
Social media has given Midrand communities a voice to complain that the local waste dump is making them ill.
LANETTE HUGHES: At the moment I’ve got 7237 submissions on my tracker.
But can they win the fight for clean air?

Script:


SCRIPT: Midstream Air
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
TX DATE: 28 March 2017

INSERT SCRIPT:
Most mornings a brown haze of air pollution hangs over Midrand, between Pretoria and Johannesburg.
It is part of the Highveld Priority Area earmarked a decade ago by government for action to rectify the worsening air quality.
Now the local landfill has become ground zero for a battle over fresh air as it faces off against residents and authorities.
CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: We hardly take the time to think about the air we breathe – but in Midrand locals have become obsessed with it as they resort to social media and messaging groups at all hours to protest about the fumes they say assault their senses – even as they try to sleep.
BOITUMELO SIBONI, IVORY PARK ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: It’s very difficult to breathe, especially in the late hours and the early mornings.
DR PHIL MAHUMA: Last night I woke up at half past one coughing and choking. because of the air.
LANETTE HUGHES: Some people vomit spontaneously when they smell it. A few weeks ago the smell was so bad that my throat started burning almost immediately and I’m still recovering from that.
CLAIRE LINK: In the last two years, residents have taken their complaints to every forum they could think of, from local to provincial to national government, the Public Protector and the media. They finally seemed to have found a champion in the Department of Environmental Affairs.
The Department, or DEA, believes it has pinpointed the source of the bad odours that regularly wash over those living there.
Grant Walters of the department’s Environmental Management Investigators, or Green Scorpions, points to the FG Landfill, owned by JSE-listed waste management company Interwaste.
GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: We’ve done extensive investigations – at all times of the day and night – these are not necessarily in the public domain at this point in time because it does form part of a criminal investigation process so that information has not been released...we’ve got the evidence.
Nestled between factories, suburbs, upmarket estates and townships, the FG Landfill used to be a stone quarry before it became a small garbage dump. In 2008, Interwaste bought it and today it is one of the largest general waste dumps in Gauteng.
Interwaste declined our offers of an on-camera interview, but earlier this month, CEO Alan Willcocks told Moneyweb that some things come with the territory in their business.
ALAN WILCOCKS, CEO INTERWASTE, FOOTAGE COURTESY MONEYWEB: Landfills smell, and that’s just party to our operations, you know, we’re not a biscuit factory. Certainly it’s a noxious environment. We believe we’ve acted very responsibly and we’ve implemented a lot of abatement measures to be good neighbours.
The Green Scorpions disagree.
GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: You have landfills all across the country...but you don’t have the impacts that we’re seeing now.
Following a year of investigation and discussions, the DEA put its foot down with the landfill in February. It issued a directive ordering Interwaste to stop the disposal of waste at the site within five days and do further studies about the possible impact of the dump.
GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: We have given Interwaste a number of opportunities to come to the department to answer to certain allegations that have been put forward. There were certain commitments that were made at various points in time...it didn’t give us what we thought we would get.
Interwaste told us in writing they’re aware of residents’ claims and therefore commissioned scientific studies that showed the landfill “does not pose elevated risk to health” although their studies do suggest odours from the site were at times “marginally above detectable limits” “localised to the landfill and its authorised buffer zone”.
GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: It involves extremely complex science...it’s at only specific points in time when there’s emissions that individuals are exposed to. It really is isolated to early early mornings or late at night...so if you are not doing your monitoring at that particular point in time, you would miss the event.
We asked the National Association for Clean Air to review Interwaste’s air quality report.
The Association was concerned that the report compares measurements over only two weeks to an annual average; and that highs and lows are averaged out, so that the true peaks are not reflected.
According to Interwaste’s own report, hydrogen sulphide as high as hundred and fifty seven micrograms per cubic metre of air was measured at a point last year. This gas with its rotten egg odour can be smelled above seven micrograms.
Other gases like sulphur dioxide detected around the dump were below acceptable South African air quality standards.
Interwaste says the spike was recorded when it was installing a landfill gas plant to capture gas and a flare that destroys some of the gas by burning it.
ALAN WILLCOCKS: The specific waste on this site is about 95% municipal waste which has a high organic content...so with the barrier system, the high moisture content and the organic content of the waste, we ended up with landfill gas being generated very quickly.
Interwaste says the liner of the dump, meant to protect soil and groundwater, caused an abundance of landfill gas.
ALAN WILLCOCKS: We learned a lot of lessons but subsequent to that to that we employed a lot of abatement measures and employed a lot of abatement measures to rectify the situation but, yes we had a lot of landfill gas generated very early in the life of the site
Musa Chamane, waste management expert at social justice NGO Groundwork has done work on over a hundred landfills, including this one, and says landfill gas plants and flares work only partially.
MUSA CHAMANE: When you insert the pipes into the body of waste – and those pipes they’re trying to trap all the gasses that are coming off from decomposition of waste which involves CO2, methane and other gases, sulphur dioxide and so on – it cannot trap everything 100% – the majority of it still goes to the atmosphere…because it’s not a closed system, it’s not happening in a tank.
Lonmin confirmed to us it used to dump sulfur-rich waste from its mines at the landfill, but stopped at the end of January...except for a “minor/insignificant spill” a month later.
The Green Scorpions have referred their investigation to the Director of Public Prosecutions to decide whether to prosecute Interwaste.
GRANT WALTERS: It really ranges from air quality offences as well as waste-related offences to the duty of care provisions that’s contained in the National Environment Management Act.
Interwaste has lodged an appeal against the directive.
Until Environment Minister Edna Molewa, the final authority, decides whether to uphold the directive, it’s business as usual at the dump.
People can make submissions to the minister until the end of March. In the meantime, residents live in limbo.
MUSA CHAMANE: Most landfills are very close to residents … chemicals and particulates, they can travel distances, they can reach you even if you are far away.
We took a flight to see the area’s air pollution that residents complain of... above the landfill the chemical rotten egg stench hit us.
Family physician Dr. Phil Mahuma lives in the Midlands Estate.
DR PHIL MAHUMA: When the evening comes, I get really depressed and anxious because you know the night is going to be terrible.
GRANT WALTERS: Even at really low levels where you would say that hydrogen sulphide won’t have a significant effect on you to the point of admission into hospital – the psychological effect is well-documented in relation to this particular matter.
Residents have discovered there’s no proven scientific link between the smell and the symptoms they complain of.
While the World Health Organisation has linked hydrogen sulphide exposure to the symptoms residents report, no research anywhere has proven the effects of long term low level exposure.
But because the symptoms come with the smell, residents feel it must mean something.
DR PHIL MAHUMA: If one comes across a noxious substance the senses warn us that that this is not something good. People will be affected differently -- different systems, different sensitivities -- then we also get different smells, so it’s a whole concoction...
Stephen Pretorius and his family live right across road from the dump.
STEVEN PRETORIUS: We get terrible headaches. When you go away, especially when you go away on holiday, all these symptoms disappear. As soon as we get back, they’re back again. I’ve even sealed the roof with concrete, because it was coming through. I’ve sealed the door. I’ve siliconed it on the outside and it’s even varnished, to seal it from coming in. We’ve got air purifiers. We’ve got masks.
CLAIRE MAWISA: When people think gas masks, they think war zone.
STEVEN PRETORIUS: And this is not the normal spraypainting gas mask, this is proper gas masks.
CLAIRE MAWISA: I have no words.
STEVEN PRETORIUS: Our concern is what’s gonna happen in the long term? You know, we’re worried.
In its appeal against the directive, Interwaste says the dump is in an industrial zone and others may well be the culprits.
It told us it cares deeply about residents, but speaking to Moneyweb, Willcocks said the complaints came from only a handful.
ALAN WILLCOCKS: We have the utmost respect for our regulator and we’re a very responsible company in terms of our activities. But they’re also suffering from this thing called social media.
In upmarket Midfield Estate, Lanette Hughes enlisted tech-savvy neighbours to devise an app that tracks complaints.
LANETTE HUGHES: You put in your name and all your details, the date of occurrence, the time that the smell is hitting you, and then we’ve got various types of smell that you can pick. We also ask them to complete the weather condition. And then they need to tick if there’s any impact on their health. At the moment, I’ve got 7237 submissions on my tracker.
CLAIRE MAWISA: From when?
LANETTE HUGHES: This is from May last year.
GRANT WALTERS: We do take all complaints very seriously. Our role as the Green Scorpions would be to ensure that there is a deterrence effect and that there’s punishment for non-compliance with environmental law.
The provincial department that licensed the landfill told us its licence had expired in 2015 and it ordered Interwaste to reapply. The matter is still in court -- Interwaste maintains the licence is valid until the court says otherwise.
In Ivory Park, Boitumelo Siboni decided to take take action, as her daughter already has breathing problems.
BOITUMELO SIBONI: She is getting eye irritations. And even my son has developed the same irritations. Myself included...I can’t really afford the medications.
Siboni is rallying young people to learn how to fight for better air.
BOITUMELO SIBONI, IVORY PARK ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: We also encourage our street vendors who do shesa nyama...and teach them about other ways of cooking.
BHEKI LANGA, IVORY PARK ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: It’s because we want to change the standard of living here.
LANETTE HUGHES: I just hope that when the minister makes her decision she’s going to first and foremost think about the victims in this case and not listen to corporate stories about businesses should continue.
CLAIRE: Because it’s affecting real people’s lives, right?
LANETTE: Yes.

It issued a directive ordering Interwaste to stop the disposal of waste at the site within five days and do further studies about the possible impact of the dump. GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: We have given Interwaste a number of opportunities to come to the department to answer to certain allegations that have been put forward. There were certain commitments that were made at various points in time...it didn’t give us what we thought we would get. Interwaste told us in writing they’re aware of residents’ claims and therefore commissioned scientific studies that showed the landfill “does not pose elevated risk to health” although their studies do suggest odours from the site were at times “marginally above detectable limits” “localised to the landfill and its authorised buffer zone”. GRANT WALTERS, DIRECTOR FOR ENFORCEMENT, DEA: It involves extremely complex science...it’s at only specific points in time when there’s emissions that individuals are exposed to. It really is isolated to early early mornings or late at night...so if you are not doing your monitoring at that particular point in time, you would miss the event. We asked the National Association for Clean Air to review Interwaste’s air quality report. The Association was concerned that the report compares measurements over only two weeks to an annual average; and that highs and lows are averaged out, so that the true peaks are not reflected. According to Interwaste’s own report, hydrogen sulphide as high as hundred and fifty seven micrograms per cubic metre of air was measured at a point last year. This gas with its rotten egg odour can be smelled above seven micrograms. Other gases like sulphur dioxide detected around the dump were below acceptable South African air quality standards. Interwaste says the spike was recorded when it was installing a landfill gas plant to capture gas and a flare that destroys some of the gas by burning it. ALAN WILLCOCKS: The specific waste on this site is about 95% municipal waste which has a high organic content...so with the barrier system, the high moisture content and the organic content of the waste, we ended up with landfill gas being generated very quickly. Interwaste says the liner of the dump, meant to protect soil and groundwater, caused an abundance of landfill gas. ALAN WILLCOCKS: We learned a lot of lessons but subsequent to that to that we employed a lot of abatement measures and employed a lot of abatement measures to rectify the situation but, yes we had a lot of landfill gas generated very early in the life of the site Musa Chamane, waste management expert at social justice NGO Groundwork has done work on over a hundred landfills, including this one, and says landfill gas plants and flares work only partially. MUSA CHAMANE: When you insert the pipes into the body of waste – and those pipes they’re trying to trap all the gasses that are coming off from decomposition of waste which involves CO2, methane and other gases, sulphur dioxide and so on – it cannot trap everything 100% – the majority of it still goes to the atmosphere…because it’s not a closed system, it’s not happening in a tank. Lonmin confirmed to us it used to dump sulfur-rich waste from its mines at the landfill, but stopped at the end of January...except for a “minor/insignificant spill” a month later. The Green Scorpions have referred their investigation to the Director of Public Prosecutions to decide whether to prosecute Interwaste. GRANT WALTERS: It really ranges from air quality offences as well as waste-related offences to the duty of care provisions that’s contained in the National Environment Management Act. Interwaste has lodged an appeal against the directive. Until Environment Minister Edna Molewa, the final authority, decides whether to uphold the directive, it’s business as usual at the dump. People can make submissions to the minister until the end of March. In the meantime, residents live in limbo. MUSA CHAMANE: Most landfills are very close to residents … chemicals and particulates, they can travel distances, they can reach you even if you are far away. We took a flight to see the area’s air pollution that residents complain of... above the landfill the chemical rotten egg stench hit us. Family physician Dr. Phil Mahuma lives in the Midlands Estate. DR PHIL MAHUMA: When the evening comes, I get really depressed and anxious because you know the night is going to be terrible. GRANT WALTERS: Even at really low levels where you would say that hydrogen sulphide won’t have a significant effect on you to the point of admission into hospital – the psychological effect is well-documented in relation to this particular matter. Residents have discovered there’s no proven scientific link between the smell and the symptoms they complain of. While the World Health Organisation has linked hydrogen sulphide exposure to the symptoms residents report, no research anywhere has proven the effects of long term low level exposure. But because the symptoms come with the smell, residents feel it must mean something. DR PHIL MAHUMA: If one comes across a noxious substance the senses warn us that that this is not something good. People will be affected differently -- different systems, different sensitivities -- then we also get different smells, so it’s a whole concoction... Stephen Pretorius and his family live right across road from the dump. STEVEN PRETORIUS: We get terrible headaches. When you go away, especially when you go away on holiday, all these symptoms disappear. As soon as we get back, they’re back again. I’ve even sealed the roof with concrete, because it was coming through. I’ve sealed the door. I’ve siliconed it on the outside and it’s even varnished, to seal it from coming in. We’ve got air purifiers. We’ve got masks. CLAIRE MAWISA: When people think gas masks, they think war zone. STEVEN PRETORIUS: And this is not the normal spraypainting gas mask, this is proper gas masks. CLAIRE MAWISA: I have no words. STEVEN PRETORIUS: Our concern is what’s gonna happen in the long term? You know, we’re worried. In its appeal against the directive, Interwaste says the dump is in an industrial zone and others may well be the culprits. It told us it cares deeply about residents, but speaking to Moneyweb, Willcocks said the complaints came from only a handful. ALAN WILLCOCKS: We have the utmost respect for our regulator and we’re a very responsible company in terms of our activities. But they’re also suffering from this thing called social media. In upmarket Midfield Estate, Lanette Hughes enlisted tech-savvy neighbours to devise an app that tracks complaints. LANETTE HUGHES: You put in your name and all your details, the date of occurrence, the time that the smell is hitting you, and then we’ve got various types of smell that you can pick. We also ask them to complete the weather condition. And then they need to tick if there’s any impact on their health. At the moment, I’ve got 7237 submissions on my tracker. CLAIRE MAWISA: From when? LANETTE HUGHES: This is from May last year. GRANT WALTERS: We do take all complaints very seriously. Our role as the Green Scorpions would be to ensure that there is a deterrence effect and that there’s punishment for non-compliance with environmental law. The provincial department that licensed the landfill told us its licence had expired in 2015 and it ordered Interwaste to reapply. The matter is still in court -- Interwaste maintains the licence is valid until the court says otherwise. In Ivory Park, Boitumelo Siboni decided to take take action, as her daughter already has breathing problems. BOITUMELO SIBONI: She is getting eye irritations. And even my son has developed the same irritations. Myself included...I can’t really afford the medications. Siboni is rallying young people to learn how to fight for better air. BOITUMELO SIBONI, IVORY PARK ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: We also encourage our street vendors who do shesa nyama...and teach them about other ways of cooking. BHEKI LANGA, IVORY PARK ENVIRONMENTAL ACTIVIST: It’s because we want to change the standard of living here. LANETTE HUGHES: I just hope that when the minister makes her decision she’s going to first and foremost think about the victims in this case and not listen to corporate stories about businesses should continue. CLAIRE: Because it’s affecting real people’s lives, right? LANETTE: Yes.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Residents of the upmarket Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand thought they were buying into a dream lifestyle ... until gases and the stench from a private landfill site started affecting their quality of life and their health. Residents of these estates and surrounding areas in Olifantsfontein and Tembisa in Midrand, have been battling for more than two years to get Interwaste to address the dangerous gases emanating from its FG Landfill site in Midrand. The source of the problem is said to be mining waste from Lonmin and possibly other mines being dumped at the landfill site. The gases being emitted from the site include hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. Those living in the area say the stench is so bad on some days that they have to fight the urge to throw up. They say they suffer regular respiratory illnesses and ailments such as nose bleeds. Lanette Hughes, who is spearheading residents' battle, says her two young children are often sick, her childhood asthma has returned and they have needed to buy air purifiers for their home. Another resident says her family suffers so much that they are nearly exclusively living in one room in their house that has an air purifier installed. Hughes and her team of volunteers are using technology to their advantage and have created an online tracker for people to record complaints. Between May 2016 and February 2017, there were a total of 4582 complaints logged. A record number of 919 complaints were logged from Midstream Estate between 1 and 13 February. They have also taken their woes to the Public Protector, where an agreement was reached in October 2016 and Interwaste, the Department of Environmental Affairs and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development were asked to make commitments to address the problems. But residents say that the commitments are not begin honoured and the situation is now worse than ever. In an attempt to work with Interwaste to solve the problems, the developers of the Midstream Estate, Bondev, purchased machinery to measure the gases in the air. Residents say that the steps that have been taken to address the problems are not working because Interwaste is not taking the necessary steps. They say, for instance, that the flares installed to burn off the gases do not have the required scrubbers installed.
metadata.Summary: Who ensures the quality of the air we breathe? This is a question that residents of the Midstream, Midlands and Randjiesfontein Estates in Midrand, Olifantsfontein and Tembisa are asking themselves in their battle for clean air. They say the Department of environmental Affairs (DEA) and the Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (GDARD) is letting them down by not clamping down on Interwaste's FG Landfill site in Midrand. They say the landfill site is emitting dangerous gases and bad odours into the air and not taking the necessary steps to prevent harm to the health of people living in the area. The large private landfill site accepts waste from mining operations by Lonmin and possibly other mine groups. Let alone the bad smell, residents say they suffer respiratory illnesses, nose bleeds and more. They have to take their children to the doctor numerous time a month. Many have costly air purifiers in their homes. An online tracking tool developed by those spearheading the battle has recorded more than 4000 complaints in less than a year. Section 24 of the Bill of Rights in the South African Constitution guarantees everyone the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being. Residents first started complaining to the DEA and GDARD in 2014 but, dissatisfied with what they saw as a lack of action, a group of residents took their case to the Public Protector's Office, which facilitated an agreement between the parties in November 2016. But, say residents, the pollution is now worse than ever and the monthly feedback meetings promised by the DEA have not happened. The DEA and GDARD were also supposed to provide the Public Protector's Office with regular feedback. We aim to interview residents of the area, representatives of the DEA and GDARD, Interwaste (owners of the landfill) and an independent air quality scientist.
